title: Chapter review: Numbers
description: Questions on the ideas in this chapter, from one star (a check of the definitions) to four stars (combining several ideas). They come in a random order each time.

questions.question: Which statement about $$0$$ matches the definitions?
options: $$0$$ is a natural number, but neither positive nor negative
$$0$$ is a negative integer, because it is less than $$1$$
$$0$$ is not an integer, because it counts nothing
questions.explanation: The natural numbers are the positive integers together with $$0$$, and $$0$$ itself is neither positive nor negative (:ref{#integers}).

questions.question: On the number line, what does it mean for one integer to be bigger than another?
options: It sits further to the right
It sits further to the left
questions.explanation: Every step to the right is one more, so the further right a number sits, the bigger it is. That is why $$-1$$ is bigger than $$-4$$, even though $$-4$$ is further from $$0$$.

questions.question: Let $$a$$ be an integer. What can be said about $$-a$$?
options: It is the opposite of $$a$$, so it is positive whenever $$a$$ is negative
questions.explanation: The minus sign means “the opposite of”, not “negative” (:ref{#opposite}). If $$a = -2$$ then $$-a = 2$$. And $$-0 = 0$$, so $$-a$$ can equal $$a$$.

questions.question: Which of these facts about adding integers is taken as a basic rule, rather than proved?
options: The sum of two negative integers is negative
questions.explanation: Commutativity and associativity are assumed, together with the facts about $$0$$ and opposites and that a sum of positive integers is positive. The other three options are all worked out from these in [Rules for addition](#rules-for-addition).

questions.question: By definition, what does $$a - b$$ mean?
questions.explanation: Subtraction is not a new operation, just adding an opposite (:ref{#subtraction}). That is why the rules for addition carry over to subtraction.

questions.question: Is $$a - b = b - a$$ for all integers $$a$$ and $$b$$?
options: Yes, because subtraction is a kind of addition and addition is commutative
No: $$a - b$$ and $$b - a$$ are opposites, so they are equal only when $$a = b$$
questions.explanation: Commutativity lets us swap $$a$$ and $$-b$$ in $$a + (-b)$$, giving $$-b + a$$, not $$b - a$$. In fact $$b - a = -(a - b)$$, and a number equals its opposite only when it is $$0$$, that is when $$a = b$$.

questions.question: Which fact does the chapter use to explain why $$-(-a) = a$$?
options: Two minus signs always cancel, which is taken as given
Since $$-a + a = 0$$, and an opposite is the only number that adds to give $$0$$, $$a$$ must be the opposite of $$-a$$
questions.explanation: If $$x + y = 0$$ then $$y = -x$$, so an opposite is the only way back to zero. Applying this to $$-a + a = 0$$ says that $$a$$ is the opposite of $$-a$$.

questions.question: Why is $$-(a + b) = -a - b$$?
options: It is the definition of the opposite of a sum
Because $$(a + b) + (-a - b)$$ regroups to $$0$$, and only the opposite of $$a + b$$ adds to it to give $$0$$
Because the minus sign can be multiplied into the bracket
It has been checked for enough examples to be sure
questions.explanation: Regrouping gives $$(a - a) + (b - b) = 0 + 0 = 0$$, and an opposite is the only way back to zero. No multiplication is needed, and checking examples never proves a rule for all integers.

questions.question: How is it shown that the sum of two negative integers is negative?
options: It is assumed as a basic fact
Write them as $$-m$$ and $$-n$$ with $$m$$, $$n$$ positive; the sum is $$-(m + n)$$, and $$m + n$$ is positive
By walking along the number line for every pair
questions.explanation: Only the fact about **positive** sums is assumed. The negative case follows from it using the opposite of a sum.

questions.question: What can be said about the sum of a positive integer and a negative integer?
options: It can be positive, negative or $$0$$
questions.explanation: With mixed signs the result can go either way: $$-5 + 11 = 6$$, $$5 + (-11) = -6$$ and $$5 + (-5) = 0$$.

questions.question: The chapter shows that $$0 \cdot a = 0$$ does not need to be assumed. Which argument does it use?
options: $$0 \cdot a + a = (0 + 1)a = a$$, then subtract $$a$$ from both sides
questions.explanation: Distributivity together with $$1 \cdot a = a$$ gives $$0 \cdot a + a = a$$, and subtracting $$a$$ leaves $$0 \cdot a = 0$$. The third option needs $$(-a)a = -(a^2)$$, which the chapter proves using $$0 \cdot a = 0$$, so it goes round in a circle. The fourth just swaps the order.

questions.question: Why is $$(-1)a = -a$$?
options: Because $$(-1)a + a = (-1 + 1)a = 0 \cdot a = 0$$, and only $$-a$$ adds to $$a$$ to give $$0$$
It is assumed as one of the basic rules
Because $$-1$$ is negative and $$a$$ keeps its size
questions.explanation: Distributivity shows $$(-1)a$$ adds to $$a$$ to give $$0$$, and an opposite is the only way back to zero. The definition of $$-a$$ (:ref{#opposite}) does not mention multiplication at all.

questions.question: Why is $$(-a)(-b) = ab$$?
options: It is one of the basic rules of multiplication
Because two negatives cancel when added
Because a minus sign can be moved out of either factor: $$(-a)(-b) = -(a(-b)) = -(-(ab)) = ab$$
Because both sides have the same size
questions.explanation: First $$-(xy) = (-x)y = x(-y)$$ is proved from distributivity. Moving each minus sign out in turn leaves two minus signs in front, and $$-(-c) = c$$.

questions.question: A product has five negative factors and two positive factors, none of them $$0$$. What is its sign?
options: It depends on the sizes of the factors
questions.explanation: Each pair of minus signs cancels, so an odd number of negative factors leaves the product negative.

questions.question: Distributivity has two forms, $$a(b + c) = ab + ac$$ and $$(b + c)a = ba + ca$$. Why does only one need to be assumed?
options: Because commutativity of multiplication turns one into the other
Because the second form is never used
Because associativity of addition turns one into the other
questions.explanation: $$(b + c)a = a(b + c) = ab + ac = ba + ca$$, using only that the order of factors does not matter.

questions.question: For an integer $$a$$ and a positive integer $$n$$, what is $$a^n$$?
questions.explanation: A power is a repeated product (:ref{#power}). The second option describes $$na$$, a repeated sum.

questions.question: Which of these is **not** a rule for powers? (Here $$m$$ and $$n$$ are positive integers.)
questions.explanation: The rules come from counting copies of $$a$$ in a **product**. A sum of powers does not combine: $$2^2 + 2^1 = 6$$, but $$2^3 = 8$$.

questions.question: If $$a$$ is a negative integer, when is $$a^n$$ positive?
questions.explanation: The product has $$n$$ negative factors, and an even number of minus signs gives a positive product, for example $$(-2)^4 = 16$$ and $$(-2)^3 = -8$$.

questions.question: Why is $$(a + b)^2$$ not usually equal to $$a^2 + b^2$$?
options: Because squaring only works for single numbers
Because expanding $$(a + b)(a + b)$$ also produces the cross terms $$ab$$ and $$ba$$, which add to $$2ab$$
It is equal, by the power of a product rule
questions.explanation: Multiplying every part of one bracket by every part of the other gives four terms, $$a^2 + ab + ba + b^2$$. As an area, a square of side $$a + b$$ contains **two** rectangles of area $$ab$$. The power of a product rule is about $$(ab)^2$$, not $$(a + b)^2$$.

questions.question: Which of these has **no** factorising formula like the others?
questions.explanation: $$a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)$$, and both differences and sums of cubes factor. A sum of squares does not factor this way.

questions.question: Which factorisation is correct?
questions.explanation: The short bracket has the same sign as the left side, and the middle term of the long bracket has the opposite sign. Expanding $$(a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)$$ makes the middle terms cancel, leaving $$a^3 + b^3$$.

questions.question: How can $$(a - b)^3$$ be found from the formula for $$(a + b)^3$$ without new work?
options: Replace $$a$$ by $$-a$$, which changes every sign
Subtract $$2b^3$$ from the cube of a sum
Replace $$b$$ by $$-b$$: the terms with an odd power of $$b$$ change sign and the rest stay the same
It cannot; it has to be expanded from scratch

questions.question: Which is the definition of an odd integer?
options: An integer that can be written as $$2n + 1$$ for some positive integer $$n$$
An integer whose last digit is $$1$$, $$3$$, $$5$$, $$7$$ or $$9$$
An integer that can be written as $$2n + 1$$ for some integer $$n$$
An integer that is not divisible by $$3$$
questions.explanation: The integer $$n$$ can be any integer (:ref{#even-odd}). Requiring $$n$$ to be positive would leave out $$1 = 2 \cdot 0 + 1$$ and every negative odd number. The last digit is a handy test, but not the definition.

questions.question: Is $$0$$ even?
options: No, because $$0$$ is neither positive nor negative
No, $$0$$ is neither even nor odd
It is both even and odd
questions.explanation: Being even means being $$2$$ times some integer (:ref{#even-odd}), and $$0 = 2 \cdot 0$$. Every integer is either even or odd, never both.

questions.question: Why is the sum of two odd integers always even?
options: Because odd plus odd is a rule of arithmetic
questions.explanation: The two leftover $$1$$s pair up with each other. Examples alone do not prove a rule for every pair, and the last option has an arithmetic slip.

questions.question: When is a product of several integers odd?
options: When at least one factor is odd
When an odd number of the factors are odd
When the number of factors is odd
questions.explanation: An even number times any integer is even, so a single even factor makes the whole product even.

questions.question: How does the chapter prove that if $$a^2$$ is even, then $$a$$ is even?
options: It is the same statement as “the square of an even integer is even”
If $$a$$ were odd, its square would be odd, which it is not; and every integer is even or odd
questions.explanation: The proof of :ref{#squares-parity-converse} rules out the wrong case using :ref{#squares-parity}. The second option is the converse of what is being proved, a different statement.

questions.question: What does $$d \mid n$$ mean?
options: $$\frac{n}{d}$$ is a fraction in lowest form
questions.explanation: $$d$$ divides $$n$$ when $$n$$ is a multiple of $$d$$ (:ref{#divides}). For example $$6 \mid -42$$, because $$-42 = 6 \cdot (-7)$$.

questions.question: Which statement is true?
questions.explanation: $$0 = d \cdot 0$$ for every $$d$$, so $$0$$ is a multiple of everything. But $$0 \mid n$$ would need $$n = 0 \cdot k = 0$$, so $$0$$ divides only $$0$$.

questions.question: Suppose $$d \mid m$$ and $$d \mid n$$. Which of these does **not** follow?
questions.explanation: Anything built from multiples of $$d$$ by adding, subtracting or multiplying is a multiple of $$d$$ (:ref{#multiples}). But that says nothing about how $$m$$ and $$n$$ relate: $$2 \mid 4$$ and $$2 \mid 6$$, yet $$4 \nmid 6$$.

questions.question: What does $$a \equiv b \pmod{d}$$ mean?
questions.explanation: Two integers are congruent modulo $$d$$ when their difference is a multiple of $$d$$ (:ref{#congruence}), like $$15$$ and $$3$$ o'clock on a $$12$$-hour clock.

questions.question: Which statement says the same as $$n \equiv 0 \pmod{d}$$?
questions.explanation: $$n \equiv 0$$ means $$d \mid n - 0$$, which is $$d \mid n$$. So “divisible by $$d$$” and “congruent to $$0$$ modulo $$d$$” are the same thing.

questions.question: In proving “if $$a \equiv b$$ and $$b \equiv c$$, then $$a \equiv c$$”, what is the key step?
options: $$(a - b) + (b - c) = a - c$$, a sum of two multiples of $$d$$
$$a = b = c$$, so their differences are $$0$$
questions.explanation: The two known differences add up to the one we want, because the $$b$$s cancel. Then :ref{#multiples} shows the sum is a multiple of $$d$$ (:ref{#congruence-equality}).

questions.question: To prove that $$a \equiv b$$ and $$x \equiv y$$ give $$ax \equiv by \pmod{d}$$, which rewriting of $$ax - by$$ does the proof use?
questions.explanation: Subtracting and adding the halfway term $$bx$$ changes one letter at a time: $$ax - bx + bx - by$$. Each part is a multiple of a known multiple of $$d$$ (:ref{#congruence-arithmetic}). The first option is wrong: expanding it gives $$ax - ay - bx + by$$.

questions.question: How is it proved that $$a \equiv b \pmod{d}$$ gives $$a^n \equiv b^n \pmod{d}$$ for every positive integer $$n$$?
options: By checking $$n = 1, 2, 3$$ and noticing the pattern
By induction: it holds for $$n = 1$$, and multiplying by $$a \equiv b$$ takes each power to the next
By the power of a power rule
questions.explanation: Proving a first case and showing each case leads to the next reaches every positive integer (:ref{#congruence-powers}). Checking a few cases is not a proof.

questions.question: Which of these is **false** in general, for a positive integer $$d$$ and integers $$a$$, $$b$$, $$c$$?
options: If $$a \equiv b$$, then $$a + c \equiv b + c \pmod{d}$$
questions.explanation: Congruences can be added and multiplied, but a common factor cannot always be cancelled (:ref{#no-cancel}). For example $$2 \cdot 3 \equiv 2 \cdot 8 \pmod{10}$$, but $$3 \not\equiv 8 \pmod{10}$$.

questions.question: Which statement says exactly the same as “if $$3 \mid a^2$$, then $$3 \mid a$$”?
questions.explanation: Turning a statement round and negating both parts gives an equivalent statement, which is how :ref{#squares-three} is proved. The first option is the converse; it happens to be true, but it is a different statement. The second is the converse turned round, so it is equivalent to the first option, not to the original.

questions.question: Why can a square never be congruent to $$2$$ modulo $$3$$?
options: Because every integer is $$\equiv 0$$, $$1$$ or $$2$$, and their squares are $$\equiv 0$$, $$1$$ and $$4 \equiv 1$$
questions.explanation: By :ref{#congruence-powers} we only need to square $$0$$, $$1$$ and $$2$$. None of the results is $$\equiv 2$$. This is the heart of the proof of :ref{#squares-three}.

questions.question: Which of these is **not** a rational number?
questions.explanation: A rational number is $$\frac{m}{n}$$ with $$m$$, $$n$$ integers and $$n \neq 0$$ (:ref{#rational}). $$7 = \frac{7}{1}$$ and $$0.03 = \frac{3}{100}$$ are rational, but $$\frac{5}{0}$$ has no meaning: no number multiplied by $$0$$ gives $$5$$.

questions.question: By definition, when is $$\frac{m}{n} = \frac{r}{s}$$?
questions.explanation: This is cross-multiplying (:ref{#cross-multiplying}). The first option is too strict: $$\frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{4}$$.

questions.question: Why does cancelling a common factor, $$\frac{am}{an} = \frac{m}{n}$$, require $$a \neq 0$$?
options: So that $$an \neq 0$$, keeping the left side a genuine fraction
It does not; the rule works for every $$a$$
questions.explanation: With $$a = 0$$ the left side would be $$\frac{0}{0}$$, which is not a fraction at all (:ref{#fraction-cancel}).

questions.question: What must be true of a fraction in lowest form?
options: Its numerator and denominator are both odd
Its numerator and denominator are not both even
questions.explanation: If both were even, $$2$$ would be a common divisor bigger than $$1$$ (:ref{#lowest-form}). One of them can still be even, as in $$\frac{2}{3}$$ or $$\frac{3}{4}$$.

questions.question: How does the chapter prove that every positive rational number has a lowest form?
options: Keep cancelling factors of $$2$$ until the numerator is odd
Cancel the greatest common divisor $$d$$; if anything bigger than $$1$$ still divided both, $$d$$ would not have been the greatest
Check every fraction with a small numerator
questions.explanation: If $$e > 1$$ divided both $$r$$ and $$s$$, then $$de$$ would be a common divisor bigger than $$d$$, a contradiction (:ref{#lowest-form-exists}).

questions.question: By definition, what is $$\frac{m}{n} + \frac{r}{s}$$?
questions.explanation: Both fractions are first rewritten with the denominator $$ns$$, then the numerators are added (:ref{#fraction-addition}). Adding tops and bottoms separately gives $$\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} = \frac{2}{4}$$, which is wrong.

questions.question: The rule for adding fractions uses particular numerators and denominators. What has to be true for this to be a sensible definition?
options: The fractions must already be in lowest form
Writing the same rational numbers as different fractions must give the same answer
questions.explanation: $$\frac{1}{2}$$ and $$\frac{2}{4}$$ are the same number, so adding either one to $$\frac{1}{3}$$ must give the same result: $$\frac{5}{6}$$ and $$\frac{10}{12}$$ are indeed equal. This can be proved in general by cross-multiplying.

questions.question: Why do all the rules from [Rules for addition](#rules-for-addition), such as $$-(a + b) = -a - b$$, hold for rational numbers without new proofs?
options: Because every rational number is an integer
Because they were proved using only commutativity, associativity, $$a + 0 = a$$ and $$a + (-a) = 0$$, which hold for rational numbers too
Because they are checked again for fractions in this section
They do not all hold for rational numbers
questions.explanation: A proof that only uses certain rules works for any numbers that obey those rules. This is one of the payoffs of proving things from a few basic rules.

questions.question: How is it shown that the sum of two positive rational numbers is positive?
options: Write them as $$\frac{m}{n}$$ and $$\frac{r}{s}$$ with $$m$$, $$n$$, $$r$$, $$s$$ positive; the sum $$\frac{ms + rn}{ns}$$ has a positive top and bottom
Because positive fractions lie to the right of $$0$$
By writing both in lowest form
questions.explanation: Sums and products of positive integers are positive, and a fraction with positive numerator and denominator is positive by definition (:ref{#positive-sum}).

questions.question: What does it mean for a number to be irrational?
questions.explanation: Irrational simply means not rational (:ref{#irrational}). A decimal that goes on forever can still be rational, like $$\frac{1}{3} = 0.333\ldots$$, and $$\sqrt{4} = 2$$ is rational.

questions.question: The proof that no rational number squares to $$2$$ is a proof by contradiction. Which fact does it contradict?
options: That $$m$$ and $$n$$ are not both even
questions.explanation: The fraction is written in lowest form, so $$m$$ and $$n$$ are not both even. The argument then shows they are both even (:ref{#sqrt-two}).

questions.question: Which of these is **not** used in the proof that no rational number squares to $$2$$?
options: Every positive rational number has a lowest form
If $$a^2$$ is even, then $$a$$ is even
questions.explanation: The proof uses :ref{#lowest-form-exists}, :ref{#squares-parity-converse} and :ref{#fraction-powers}, together with cross-multiplying. Congruences are only needed for the version with $$3$$, through :ref{#squares-three}.

questions.question: To prove that no rational number squares to $$3$$, what replaces the rule “if $$a^2$$ is even then $$a$$ is even”?
options: If $$a^2$$ is odd, then $$a$$ is odd
questions.explanation: The proof (:ref{#sqrt-three}) has the same shape as for $$2$$, with :ref{#squares-three} doing the job of the even-squares rule.

questions.question: Why is $$0!$$ defined to be $$1$$?
options: So that $$n! = n \cdot (n - 1)!$$ still holds when $$n = 1$$
Because the product of no numbers is $$0$$
questions.explanation: Taking $$n = 1$$ in $$n! = n \cdot (n - 1)!$$ gives $$1! = 1 \cdot 0!$$, which only works if $$0! = 1$$ (:ref{#factorial}).

questions.question: What does $$\binom{m}{n}$$ count?
options: The ways to arrange $$m$$ things in a row
The ways to choose $$n$$ things out of $$m$$, in order
The ways to choose $$n$$ things out of $$m$$, when the order doesn't matter
questions.explanation: For example, there are $$\binom{4}{2} = 6$$ ways to pick $$2$$ toppings from $$4$$ (:ref{#binomial}).

questions.question: Why is $$\binom{m}{n} = \binom{m}{m - n}$$?
options: Choosing the $$n$$ things to take is the same as choosing the $$m - n$$ things to leave behind
questions.explanation: The counting reason is backed up by the formula: the two factorials in the denominator just swap places (:ref{#binomial-symmetry}).

questions.question: Which identity is Pascal's rule?
questions.explanation: In Pascal's triangle, each entry is the sum of the two entries just above it (:ref{#pascal}). The last option is the symmetry rule, not Pascal's rule.

questions.question: What is a multiplicative inverse of a rational number $$a$$?
questions.explanation: An inverse undoes multiplying, just as an opposite undoes adding (:ref{#inverse}). The first and third options describe the opposite.

questions.question: Why does $$0$$ have no multiplicative inverse?
options: Because $$0 \cdot b = 0$$ for every $$b$$, so it is never $$1$$
Because it was left out of the definition
questions.explanation: An inverse $$b$$ would need $$0 \cdot b = 1$$, which never happens. That is the real reason we can't divide by zero.

questions.question: How is it shown that $$ab = 1$$ forces $$b = a^{-1}$$?
options: Multiply both sides by $$a^{-1}$$ and regroup: $$a^{-1}(ab) = (a^{-1}a)b = b$$
It is part of the definition of an inverse
questions.explanation: The proof (:ref{#inverse-unique}) mirrors the fact that an opposite is the only way back to zero. Dividing would assume what is being set up.

questions.question: Why must $$a = 0$$ or $$b = 0$$ when $$ab = 0$$?
questions.explanation: A non-zero $$a$$ has an inverse, and multiplying through by it leaves $$b = 0$$ (:ref{#zero-product}). Both being $$0$$ is possible but not required.

questions.question: For rational numbers with $$b \neq 0$$, how is $$\frac{a}{b}$$ defined?
options: The number of times $$b$$ fits into $$a$$
questions.explanation: Dividing by $$b$$ undoes multiplying by $$b$$, which is what multiplying by $$b^{-1}$$ does (:ref{#quotient}).

questions.question: Why does dividing by a fraction amount to multiplying by its flip?
options: It is a shortcut with no reason behind it
Because dividing by $$\frac{r}{s}$$ means multiplying by its inverse, and the inverse of $$\frac{r}{s}$$ is $$\frac{s}{r}$$
Because the numerator and denominator can always be swapped
questions.explanation: By :ref{#quotient} dividing means multiplying by the inverse, and :ref{#inverse-exists} shows that flipping a non-zero fraction gives its inverse.

questions.question: Cross-multiplying appears twice in the chapter. What is the difference between the two?
options: There is none; it is stated twice for emphasis
The first is for positive fractions only
For fractions of integers it is the definition of equality; for quotients of rational numbers it is a theorem, proved using inverses
The first is a theorem and the second is a definition
questions.explanation: Equality of $$\frac{m}{n}$$ and $$\frac{r}{s}$$ is defined by cross-multiplying (:ref{#cross-multiplying}). Once quotients are defined as $$ab^{-1}$$, the same rule can be proved (:ref{#cross-multiplying-rational}).

questions.question: When can $$ab = ac$$ be cancelled to $$b = c$$?
questions.explanation: A non-zero $$a$$ has an inverse to multiply by (:ref{#cancel-product}). Without that condition it fails: $$0 \cdot 2 = 0 \cdot 5$$, but $$2 \neq 5$$.

questions.question: What is assumed about $$x$$ whenever $$\frac{1}{x - 2}$$ appears?
questions.explanation: A denominator can never be $$0$$, so letters in denominators only take values that keep every denominator non-zero.

questions.question: How is $$\frac{x^n - 1}{x - 1} = x^{n-1} + \cdots + x + 1$$ proved, for $$x \neq 1$$?
options: By cross-multiplying, then expanding $$(x - 1)(x^{n-1} + \cdots + 1)$$ so that every middle power cancels
By cancelling $$x - 1$$ from top and bottom
questions.explanation: Cross-multiplying turns the question into one about products, which can be expanded. Only $$x^n$$ and $$-1$$ survive (:ref{#sum-of-powers}).

questions.question: To prove “$$P$$ exactly when $$Q$$”, what has to be shown?
options: That $$P$$ leads to $$Q$$, and $$Q$$ leads to $$P$$
questions.explanation: “Exactly when” claims both directions, so both must be proved, as in the proof of :ref{#cross-multiplying-rational}.

questions.question: What does a proof by contradiction do?
options: Assumes the statement is false and shows this leads to something impossible
Finds an example where the statement fails
Proves the statement for small cases first
questions.explanation: For example, :ref{#sqrt-two} supposes a rational square root of $$2$$ exists and shows its numerator and denominator would have to be both even, which is impossible for a fraction in lowest form.

questions.question: A rule has been checked for a thousand pairs of integers and always works. What does this establish?
options: That it is true for all integers
That it is true for all integers up to a thousand
Only that it holds for those pairs; a proof is needed for every case
That it is probably an axiom
questions.explanation: Checking cases can find a mistake but never covers every integer. That is why the chapter proves each rule from a few basic ones.
